newsitem.title: USA: FDA proposes clear and simple labels for OTC drugs.
newsitem.headline: FDA proposes clear and simple labels for OTC drugs.

text.p: Over-the-counter drugs would have labels as clear and as simple as the new standardised food labels under a proposal Wednesday by the Food and Drug Administration.

"This proposal is the latest effort by FDA to give consumers accurate, reliable information about products that affect their health," said outgoing FDA Commissioner David Kessler. The proposal is one of Kessler's final acts before stepping down Friday.
The new regulations would require standardised information, an easier-to-read format, and simpler language in OTC drugs labels. These drugs do not require a doctor's prescription.
For instance, labels will say "lung" instead of "pulmonary," or "hole in" instead of "perforation of."
"The information on the new, much more understandable labels will help consumers to choose the right medication and avoid harmful mistakes," said Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala.

The industry has worked with FDA on the proposal and will not oppose the regulation, said Meg Grattan, a spokeswoman for the Nonprescription Drug Manufacturers Association. The proposal "will allow manufacturers necessary flexibility" to make labels more understandable, she said.
The public has 120 days to comment on the proposal. Once instituted, manufacturers will have about two years to phase in new labels.

Dr. Sidney Wolfe, executive director of Public Citizen's Health Research Group, a consumer organisation, called FDA's proposal "an important move," and said it might help consumers avoid the pitfalls of taking medication without a physician's guidance.
The industry estimated that the label changes will cost $100 million but an FDA economic estimate put the cost at under $20 million. OTC sales are about $18 billion a year.

Federal health officials recently worked out a plan with the pharmaceutical industry to distribute leaflets along with prescription drugs that will give more information on proper use of the medication.
